newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia army says 300 dead in clashes - report.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia army says 300 dead in clashes - report.

text.p: A senior Indonesian army officer said about 300 people were killed in recent ethnic violence in the province of West Kalimantan on Borneo island, the Media Indonesia newspaper reported on Tuesday.

"It's not true that the number of victims killed reached more than 1,000, like it was quoted in an English-language newspaper in Jakarta. The number of people killed was about 300 people," Major-General Zacky Anwar Makarim, assistant to the army chief of staff for security affairs, was quoted as saying.
The paper gave no further details on the deaths and Makarim did not name the English-language newspaper.
The Indonesian Observer, an English-language daily, has reported that between 1,000 and 2,000 people died in weeks of fighting between ethnic Dayaks and migrants from Madura island off East Java.
Military officials and residents in the province had previously said at least 12 people died over the past six weeks.
Clashes erupted in late December, apparently after a fight over a girl, and lasted until early February before the army deployed about 3,000 troops to separate the warring parties.
Most Dayaks are Christians while the Maduran migrants are Moslems.
Armed Forces Chief General Feisal Tanjung on Tuesday refused to comment on the newspaper reports.
"The rioting is over, except if a few crazy people want to start it again," he told reporters without elaborating.

Jakarta has restricted the movement of journalists in West Kalimantan, a jungle-clad province that borders Malaysia's Sarawak state, making independent confirmation of the death toll difficult to establish.
A report in The Australian newspaper on Tuesday quoted local sources as saying some 600 Madurese have been killed by local Dayaks while dozens of Dayaks had been shot by soldiers.
Sporadic ethnic and religious rioting has struck other parts of mainly Moslem Indonesia since October, especially on the main island of Java. At least 14 people have died in those incidents.

Political analysts say the true death toll in West Kalimantan has been suppressed to stop the spread of the ethnic violence and to avoid international criticism of the number of people killed by the army.
"I don't buy this 2,000 figure," said one diplomat following the situation. "But I think it's somewhere above 300."
Another diplomat said the military appeared to be softening up the public for a much higher death toll in the violence.
"Our impression is that they are gradually softening people up for a big number and that if they are admitting 300 it is safe to assume there are more than that," the diplomat said.
"It is very hard to get a good number on this, but it doesn't seem to be out of the bounds of what is possible," the diplomat said, commenting on the Australian report.

The initial riots broke out from what police said was a fight between Dayak and Maduran youths over a girl at a concert in Sanggau Ledo, about 95 km (60 miles) north of Pontianak, the provincial capital.
Fighting later spread to other parts of West Kalimantan.
Residents say troops still guard several towns even though calm has gradually returned to the province.
Some military officials have said they will wait for the results of an investigation by the official National Commission on Human Rights before commenting on the situation.

Political analysts say the commission, which has been brought in to help mediate between the two ethnic groups, had a good track record in investigating a number of recent riots and outbreaks of ethnic and religious violence.
